title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text: This report examines whether Agreeableness predicts responses to the personality item “Get angry easily” using ordinal logistic regression. The analysis uses the Big Five Inventory (BFI) dataset.

library(tidyverse)
library(psych)
library(ordinal)
library(readxl)
library(ggeffects)
library(broom)
library(gt)

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
The BFI data contain 25 personality items from 2,800 people, with five items measuring each of the Big Five personality traits. Each item is answered on a 6-point scale ranging from Very inaccurate to Very accurate.
The selected outcome is C4, “Do things in a half-way manner,” an item measuring Conscientiousness. The predictor is the Neuroticism subscale score, calculated as the mean of N1 to N5.
I predict that higher Neuroticism scores will be associated with higher responses to C4. Individuals with higher Neuroticism may experience greater emotional instability, which could be associated with difficulty maintaining consistent task completion. Because C4 is reverse-keyed, higher responses indicate lower Conscientiousness.

0.3 Data preparation

0.3.1 Define response labels

labels <- c(
  "Very inaccurate",
  "Moderately inaccurate",
  "Slightly inaccurate",
  "Slightly accurate",
  "Moderately accurate",
  "Very accurate"
)



0.3.2 Score the Big Five subscales

keys <- list(
  Agreeableness = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

scores_obj <- scoreItems(
  keys,
  bfi_data,
  totals = FALSE,
  min = 1,
  max = 6
)

# Extract the five personality scores
scores <- as.data.frame(scores_obj$scores)

# Add personality scores to the original dataset
bfi_data <- bind_cols(bfi_data, scores)

# Inspect the calculated scores

bfi_data$highest <- factor(

1.2 How the predictor relates to the responses
We can also visualize how the predictor relates to the responses, seeing how each person’s Neuroticism score relates to their C4 response. Because many people have the same Neuroticism score and the same C4 response, we use geom_jitter to spread out the overlapping points.









The outcome takes only six values. A good ordinal logistic regression model should predict a probability for each of those six ordered response categories, rather than a specific decimal average that is not an available response option.

1.3 An unordered outcome
Each person’s dominant trait (their highest of the five subscale scores) is a set of categories with no built-in order. Being highest on Openness is not “more” than being highest on Agreeableness. An outcome like this requires a baseline-category (multinomial) model, such as nnet::multinom(), rather than clm().
Here we can see how many people have each trait as their highest.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
section: 4.1 4b. Comparing and interpreting the chosen model
text:
4.1 4b. Comparing and interpreting the chosen model
The slope, beta = 0.44, is on the latent logit scale. A one-point increase in Neuroticism changes the cumulative log-odds of responding at or below each C4 threshold by -0.44. Because C4 is reverse-keyed, higher responses indicate lower Conscientiousness. Therefore, a positive slope indicates that higher Neuroticism is associated with responses reflecting lower Conscientiousness, whereas a negative slope indicates an association with responses reflecting higher Conscientiousness.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
7.1 7a. Predicted category probabilities









The stacked area plot shows how the predicted probabilities of the six C4 response categories change across the observed range of Neuroticism. At each Neuroticism value, the probabilities of all six response categories sum to 1. The distribution of responses shifts across the Neuroticism scale, illustrating how Neuroticism is associated with the likelihood of selecting different C4 response categories.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
section: 7.2 7b. Coefficient plot of cumulative odds ratios
text:
7.2 7b. Coefficient plot of cumulative odds ratios
The plot shows the shared proportional-odds odds ratio for Neuroticism alongside the five threshold-specific odds ratios from Part 6. It therefore provides a visual comparison of the shared effect and the threshold-specific effects, offering an additional way to assess the proportional-odds assumption.

3.1 Define response labels

labels <- c(
  "Very inaccurate",
  "Moderately inaccurate",
  "Slightly inaccurate",
  "Slightly accurate",
  "Moderately accurate",
  "Very accurate"

3.2 Score the Big Five subscales
The negatively keyed items are reverse-scored by scoreItems() when the minus sign is included in the key.

keys <- list(
  Agreeableness = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

scores_obj <- scoreItems(
  keys,
  bfi_data,
  totals = FALSE,
  min = 1,
  max = 6
)

scores <- as_tibble(scores_obj$scores)

4.2 How the predictor relates to the responses
We can visualize how each person’s Neuroticism score relates to their C4 response. Because many people have the same Neuroticism score and C4 response, geom_jitter() spreads out overlapping points.

plot_jitter <- ggplot(
  data,
  aes(x = Neuroticism, y = as.numeric(C4), colour = C4)

The outcome takes only six ordered values. An ordinal logistic regression model predicts the probability of each of those six response categories rather than treating the outcome as a continuous decimal score.


4.3 An unordered outcome
Each person’s dominant trait (their highest of the five subscale scores) is a set of categories with no built-in order. Being highest on Openness is not “more” than being highest on Agreeableness. An outcome like this requires a baseline-category (multinomial) model, such as nnet::multinom(), rather than clm().

trait_scores <- data |>
  select(
    Agreeableness,
    Conscientiousness,
    Extraversion,
    Neuroticism,
    Openness
  )

data$highest <- factor(
  names(trait_scores)[
    max.col(as.matrix(trait_scores), ties.method = "first")
  ],
  levels = names(trait_scores)
)

ordered_dat <- data |>
  count(highest) |>
  mutate(highest = fct_reorder(highest, n))

unordered_plot <- ggplot(ordered_dat, aes(highest, n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "maroon") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Dominant trait: five categories with no order",

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
5 2. Cumulative probabilities
A cumulative probability is the probability of responding with a specific response category (j) or lower. With six ordered categories, there are five non-trivial cumulative probabilities to model. The cumulative probability of the sixth category is 100%, so it does not provide a finite cumulative odds or log-odds value.

obs_tab <- data |>
  count(C4, .drop = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    Probability = n / sum(n),
    CumulativeProbability = cumsum(Probability),
    CumulativeOdds = if_else(
      CumulativeProbability < 1,
      CumulativeProbability / (1 - CumulativeProbability),
      NA_real_
    ),
    Cumulative_Logodds = if_else(
      CumulativeProbability < 1,
      qlogis(CumulativeProbability),
      NA_real_
    )
  )

obs_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    C4 = "Category in C4 (j)",
    n = "n",
    Probability = "P(Y = j)",
    CumulativeProbability = "P(Y ≤ j)",
    CumulativeOdds = "Odds of ≤ j",
    Cumulative_Logodds = "Log-odds of ≤ j"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Probability, CumulativeProbability), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(CumulativeOdds, Cumulative_Logodds), decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")

Each cumulative probability splits the response scale into two groups: responses at or below category j and responses above it. The ordinal logistic regression model estimates all five cumulative comparisons simultaneously while accounting for the natural ordering of the six response categories.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
section: 6 3. The model with a centred predictor
text:
6 3. The model with a centred predictor
We centred the Neuroticism subscale score so that the thresholds describe a person with average Neuroticism (3.16), rather than a person with a score of 0 on the original 1–6 scale. Centring changes the thresholds but does not change the slope.
In the clm() cumulative-logit parameterization, the cumulative logit is expressed as a threshold minus the linear predictor. Therefore, a positive Neuroticism coefficient indicates greater odds of responding above a given threshold; a negative coefficient indicates lower odds of responding above a threshold.

# Null model: thresholds only, no predictors.
null <- clm(C4 ~ 1, data = data, link = "logit")

# One-predictor proportional-odds model.
one_pred <- clm(C4 ~ neuroticism_c, data = data, link = "logit")

summary(one_pred)

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
7 4. Null model versus one-predictor model
The null model has thresholds only. With no predictors, its thresholds reproduce the observed cumulative log-odds from Section 2.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five

8 5. Checking proportional odds
The ordinal logistic regression model assumes a shared slope for Neuroticism across all five cumulative thresholds. In other words, the effect of Neuroticism is assumed to be the same across the different divisions of the six ordered C4 response categories.
The nominal_test() function evaluates this assumption by fitting a model that allows Neuroticism to have a separate effect across thresholds and comparing it with the proportional-odds model using a likelihood ratio test. If the separate effects do not significantly improve model fit, the proportional-odds assumption is supported.

nt <- nominal_test(one_pred)
nt

Neuroticism: OR = 1.553, 95% CI [1.464, 1.648], p = <2e-16. Each one-point increase in Neuroticism multiplies the odds of responding above any threshold (for example, “Slightly accurate or higher” versus lower responses) by 1.553, assuming proportional odds.
An odds ratio is not a change in the number of categories, and it is not a ratio of probabilities. The table below translates the model into probabilities. It uses the threshold between Slightly inaccurate and Slightly accurate, so it shows the probability of endorsing the C4 item at or above “Slightly accurate.”

# Threshold between "Slightly inaccurate" and "Slightly accurate".
# This is the third threshold: th[3].

neuroticism_values <- c(3, 4, 5, 6)

# Under clm's cumulative-logit parameterization:
# logit[P(Y <= j)] = threshold_j - beta * centred_predictor.
logodds_lower <- as.numeric(th[3]) - b * (neuroticism_values - neuroticism_bar)

# Probability of responding above the third threshold.
prob <- 1 - plogis(logodds_lower)

# Odds of responding above the third threshold.
odds <- prob / (1 - prob)

prob_tab <- tibble(
  Neuroticism = neuroticism_values,
  Prob = prob,
  Odds = odds
)

prob_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Prob = "P(Slightly accurate or higher)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Prob, Odds), decimals = 3)

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
11 8. Results paragraph
We fitted a cumulative logit ordinal regression model predicting responses to “Do things in a half-way manner” from mean-centred Neuroticism (N = 2,774). The model including Neuroticism significantly improved fit over the null model, χ²(1) = 218.2, p < .001, with ΔAIC = -216.2. The estimated cumulative odds ratio was 1.553, 95% CI [1.464, 1.648], p < .001. Thus, each one-point increase in Neuroticism was associated with higher odds of selecting a higher C4 response under the proportional-odds model. Because C4 is reverse-keyed in the Conscientiousness scale, higher C4 responses indicate lower Conscientiousness.
The proportional-odds test provided evidence against the shared-slope assumption, χ²(4) = 12.48, p = 0.0141. The threshold-specific model therefore provides a more flexible description of the association. The predicted probability of responding “Slightly accurate or higher” under the proportional-odds model was 0.245 at a Neuroticism score of 3 and 0.548 at a score of 6. These probabilities are illustrative because the proportional-odds assumption was not supported.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
12 Answers to the assignment questions

12.1 Question 1: Describe your outcome and predictor.
The outcome variable was C4 (“Do things in a half-way manner”), an ordinal item measuring Conscientiousness, with six ordered response categories ranging from “Very inaccurate” to “Very accurate.” The predictor was Neuroticism, calculated as the mean score across the five Neuroticism items (N1–N5). Higher C4 responses indicate greater agreement with the statement and, because C4 is reverse-keyed in the Conscientiousness scale, reflect lower Conscientiousness.


12.2 Question 2: The N analysed, and whether any categories were sparse or collapsed.

nrow(data)

[1] 2774

table(data$C4)


      Very inaccurate Moderately inaccurate   Slightly inaccurate 
                  769                   794                   472 
    Slightly accurate   Moderately accurate         Very accurate 
                  448                   228                    63 


The analysis included 2774 complete observations. The six response categories were retained as ordered categories; no categories were collapsed. The least frequent category contained 63 responses (2.27% of the sample). It was less frequent than the other categories but was not empty.


12.3 Question 3: The LRT comparing M0 and M1 (χ², df, p) and the ΔAIC.

lr_stat <- lrt$LR.stat[2]
lr_df <- lrt$df[2]
lr_p <- lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]

  Delta_AIC = delta_aic
)

The ΔAIC (AIC for the Neuroticism model minus AIC for the null model) was -216.2. The negative ΔAIC indicates that the Neuroticism model had a lower AIC and was preferred over the null model.
